title: Evil is a lack (ST I.48–49)
hook: evil is not a thing, but the absence of a good that should be there

segments.voice: Yesterday, creation, every moment: for Thomas, God doesn't just start the world, he keeps giving it being, like the sun keeping the air bright. Your line was held now. What did your hand rest on when you remembered? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

A sweater comes out of the closet in the fall with a hole in the sleeve. You can point to the hole. You can push a finger through it. It's real enough to ruin the sweater. But try to take the hole out and set it on the table by itself. There's nothing to pick up. The hole is only where wool should be and isn't. Which leads to a hard question, one that follows straight from yesterday. If God holds every created thing in being, every moment, does he hold evil in being too? Thomas answers with today's word: privation.
screen: `A HOLE IN THE SLEEVE.` → `NOTHING TO PICK UP.` → `DOES GOD HOLD EVIL IN BEING?`

segments.voice: Thomas starts from Genesis. In the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." If everything that has being is good, then evil can't be one more thing on the list. So, following Augustine, Thomas says evil is a privation: the absence of a good that should be there. Not just any absence. That part is careful. A stone can't see, and nothing is wrong with the stone. A person who has lost their sight is missing something a human eye is meant to have. Same lack of seeing; only one is a privation. Evil is always a lack measured against what a thing is for. Then a second surprise. Evil, Thomas says, can only exist in something good. A hole needs a sweater. Rot needs a tree. A lie needs a mind made for truth. Even the worst cruelty is done by a real person, with real gifts, bent away from what those gifts are for. And this is why Thomas says there is no supreme evil, no dark rival to God. A perfect evil would have to destroy every good, and so would destroy itself, with nothing left to be bad. Now the warning, because this teaching is easy to hear wrong. A lack is not unreal. People fall into holes. A missing kindness, a missing truth, a missing parent: these do terrible damage. Thomas isn't shrinking evil. He's saying it has no foothold of its own. Paul's line in Romans makes the same shape practical: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good." You don't fight a hole by staring at it. You fill it.
screen: `EVERYTHING GOD MADE IS GOOD.` · `EVIL: A GOOD THAT SHOULD BE THERE.` · `A HOLE NEEDS A SWEATER.` · `A LACK IS STILL REAL.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL BY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name something missing, not something bad. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing in your life right now that feels wrong. A strained friendship. A habit you're ashamed of. A mess at work. Instead of naming it as a bad thing, ask Thomas's question: what good should be here, and isn't? Patience, maybe. Honesty. Rest. A conversation that never happened. Name the missing good, plainly, in a word or two. Then stay with it. Notice that a missing good can be supplied, a little at a time. If you pray, you can ask God for that one good by name. The bell holds the time.
Privation. The absence of a good that should be there. For Thomas, that is what evil is: not a thing God made, but a lack in something good. Today's word.
Your line: a hole, not a thing. Today, when something goes wrong, name the good that's missing, and add one bit of it yourself. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Catholic teachers often explain evil, following Augustine and Thomas, as the absence of a good that ought to be present, and the idea comes up in homilies and classes on suffering and sin.

like a hole in a sweater: the lack needs a good subject to be a lack in.

fork.setup: you're Thomas. a student asks: if God made everything, and evil is real, didn't God make evil? what do you answer?
options: yes: God made evil along with everything else.
evil isn't a made thing; it's a good missing where it should be.
there's a supreme evil that made it, a rival to God.
fork.reveal: Thomas, following Augustine, calls evil a privation: not a thing on the list of creation, but a lack in something good. and he rejects any supreme evil.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: a lack, a being-deprived of something.

trapdoor: what you thought: evil is a dark force, a thing out there.
what it means: evil is a privation, the absence of a good that should be present, and it can only exist in something good.
what a scholar hears: Thomas separates mere absence from privation: not seeing is no evil in a stone, but blindness is a lack in an animal.

sources.quoted: And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good.
Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: evil as privation of a due good, following Augustine (I.48.1); the stone/animal sight example distinguishing absence from privation (I.48.3 and 48.5); the subject of evil is good (I.48.3); no supreme evil, since a total evil would destroy itself (I.49.3).
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Genesis 1:31 and Romans 12:21.
The teach explicitly warns against hearing privation as 'evil isn't real'; a Keeper may want to check that the treatment of suffering is pastorally sound.
